title: Computer Fundamentals
lines: This is the largest topic in USAT-CS. Expect questions on the parts of a computer and what each does, types of memory, number conversions (binary, octal, hexadecimal), two's complement, character codes, kinds of software and translators, operating system jobs, and everyday office tasks such as copying spreadsheet formulas.
## Hardware and the processing cycle
- Input devices: keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, webcam, barcode reader. Output devices: monitor, printer, speaker, plotter (large drawings). A touchscreen is both input and output.
- The CPU has an arithmetic logic unit (ALU), which does arithmetic and comparisons, and a control unit (CU), which fetches and decodes instructions and sends control signals.

- Registers are tiny, very fast stores inside the CPU: the program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction; the instruction register (IR) holds the current one; MAR and MDR hold a memory address and the data moving to or from it.
- The machine (instruction) cycle is fetch → decode → execute.
- Buses: the address bus carries addresses from the CPU to memory (one way); the data bus carries data both ways; the control bus carries signals such as read, write and clock.
- An n-bit address bus can reach 2ⁿ memory locations. Clock speed is measured in hertz (GHz for modern processors).
## Memory and storage
| Type | Volatile? | Notes
| RAM | yes | main memory for running programs; read and write
| ROM | no | holds the start-up (boot) program; normally read only
| Cache | yes | small, fast SRAM between the CPU and RAM
| Secondary storage | no | hard disk, SSD, USB flash drive, CD/DVD, magnetic tape
- Speed from fastest to slowest: registers → cache → RAM → secondary storage. Cost per byte falls in the same order.
- PROM can be written once; EPROM is erased by ultraviolet light; EEPROM and flash memory are erased electrically.
- Magnetic tape allows only sequential access, so finding one record in the middle is slow; disks allow direct (random) access.
- Units: 1 nibble = 4 bits; 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 KB = 1,024 bytes; 1 MB = 1,024 KB; then GB, TB.
## Number systems
| System | Base | Digits
| Binary | 2 | 0, 1
| Octal | 8 | 0-7
| Decimal | 10 | 0-9
| Hexadecimal | 16 | 0-9 and A-F (A = 10 … F = 15)
- Binary to decimal: add the place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 under each 1.
- Decimal to binary: divide by 2 repeatedly and read the remainders from bottom to top.
- Binary to octal: group bits in threes from the right. Binary to hexadecimal: group bits in fours from the right.
> Convert decimal 58 to binary, octal and hexadecimal.
> Hexadecimal: 0011 | 1010 → 3 A, so (3A)₁₆. Check: 3 × 16 + 10 = 58.
## Negative numbers and characters
- In two's complement, a negative number is made by inverting all bits of the positive number and adding 1. The leftmost bit is the sign bit: 1 means negative.
- An 8-bit two's complement number ranges from −128 to +127.
> Write −6 in 8-bit two's complement.
> Invert every bit: 11111001.
- ASCII is a 7-bit code with 128 characters: 'A' = 65, 'a' = 97, '0' = 48. Extended ASCII uses 8 bits (256 characters). Unicode gives codes to the characters of nearly all languages, including Urdu.
! Group bits from the right, not the left, and pad the leftmost group with 0s. 1101 is (D)₁₆, but 11010 is 0001 1010 = (1A)₁₆.
## Software
- System software runs the computer: the operating system, utility programs (antivirus, disk defragmenter, backup, file compression) and language translators.
- Application software does a user's task: word processor, spreadsheet, web browser, accounting package.

- Translators: an assembler turns assembly language into machine code; a compiler translates the whole high-level program at once and lists errors at the end; an interpreter translates and runs one line at a time and stops at the first error.
- Levels of language: machine language (binary) and assembly language are low level; C, C++, Java and Python are high level.
## Operating systems

- Jobs of the OS: process management (which program gets the CPU), memory management, file management, device management through drivers, security (user accounts and permissions), and the user interface (GUI or command line).
- Types: single-user, multi-user, batch, real-time (controls machines that must respond at once), and time-sharing.
- In Windows, files deleted from the hard disk go to the Recycle Bin and can be restored until it is emptied. Files deleted from a USB flash drive are normally removed for good.
- Cut and Paste moves a file; Copy and Paste duplicates it.
## Office basics

- Word processor: Find and Replace changes words throughout a document; Mail Merge combines one letter with a data list to make a copy for each person; a page break starts a new page; justified alignment lines text up with both margins.
- Spreadsheet: formulas start with =. When a formula is copied, relative references shift by the same rows and columns; a $ sign fixes the column or row written after it.
> Cell C1 holds =A1*B$1. It is copied to D3. What formula appears in D3?
> The move is 1 column right and 2 rows down.
> A1 becomes B3. In B$1 the column shifts (B → C) but the row is fixed, giving C$1.
> D3 holds =B3*C$1.
! A $ fixes only what directly follows it: $A1 fixes column A, A$1 fixes row 1, $A$1 fixes both.
## Quick check
- Which register holds the address of the next instruction? (program counter)
- Which memory loses its data when power is off? (RAM)
- (101101)₂ in decimal? (45)
- (2F)₁₆ in decimal? (47)
- How many locations can a 16-bit address bus reach? (65,536)
- Which translator runs a program line by line? (interpreter)
